source.title: J-Anchor: Defending Against Prefill Attacks via J-Space Selective Refusal Restoration
source.authors: Run Yang; Bei-Di Zhao; Xiao-Xiao Li

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether forced assistant prefixes bypass refusal by measuring harmful-completion rates under fixed and deep prefill attacks, using the study’s own evaluation setup.
record.gate_note: The study reports prefill attack results and token-position refusal/harmfulness signal dynamics. Results for J-Anchor and its competing defenses are not cataloged as evidence for the claim: they evaluate those defenses rather than the effect of prefilling itself. The fixed-prefill table is flattened and its values cannot be assigned reliably to every model and benchmark, so only clearly assignable deep-prefill base-model results are included. Cited results from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study measures harmful-completion ASR when prefilling a compliant opening (fixed and deep k=500) on four undefended instruction-tuned models, against a clean no-prefill baseline. This bears directly on V4. Its prefill protocol follows Qi et al., but it uses different models, benchmarks and a HarmBench-classifier judge.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Refusal weakens faster than harmfulness recognition as prefill tokens accumulate ('refusal-state erosion'). J-Anchor, a training-free defense that restores the pre-attack refusal state, cuts fixed- and deep-prefill ASR to a few percent while largely preserving benign behavior and reasoning.
record.recipe_differences: Studies forced assistant-prefix attacks and a training-free J-lens restoration defense; it does not fine-tune on harmful or benign examples or measure aligned-versus-base KL divergence.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different attack settings (fixed versus deep prefill, with deep prefill k=500), four model backbones, and multiple harmful benchmarks. Its text states that deep prefill raises base-model ASR; fixed-prefill table values could not be assigned reliably from the flattened text.

fits_no_version.finding: The J-lens refusal signal declines toward the benign baseline over the prefill, while the harmfulness signal stays above baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under prefill attacks, internal refusal representations erode faster than harmfulness representations.

fits_no_version.finding: Failed attacks show stronger refusal-signal recovery during decoding.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-signal recovery during decoding predicts failure of prefill attacks.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the ASR results. The fixed-prefill table text is flattened, preventing reliable assignment of several values to their model and benchmark conditions. The paper reports deep-prefill ASR and qualitative signal dynamics but does not provide paired clean-versus-prefill values for every model and benchmark in the cited deep-prefill tables.
record.rows_left_out: Fixed-prefill ASR entries from Table 1 and Table 4 were omitted because the flattened text does not support reliable model-by-benchmark assignment. J-Anchor and comparator-defense results were omitted because they evaluate defense methods rather than the effect of prefilling itself.

untested.parts: No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Suffix attacks and decoding-parameter changes are not tested; only prefilling is.
No parameter or rank localization of safety.
No analysis of the data or objective causing shallowness.
No training-based deepening. J-Anchor is an inference-time steering defense.

missing.what: Fixed-prefill undefended ASR against clean, per model and benchmark. Llama: SR 1.9→65.2, AB 6.0→65.0, HB 10.1→54.1. Gemma-4: SR 0.0→82.7, AB 1.0→89.0, HB 5.0→80.5. Qwen3.5: SR 0.0→77.3, AB 1.0→79.0, HB 1.3→64.2. Qwen3-8B: SR 1.0→67.7, AB 0.0→82.0, HB 13.8→69.2. These are assignable: Table 3's no-defense column and the text range 54.1–89.0% confirm them.
Judge robustness: under the DeepSeek-Flash judge, undefended ASR stays high under fixed (~53–94%) and deep (~94–99%) prefill.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is this study; it cites Qi et al. 2025 and follows its deep-prefill definition. The record's claim that the fixed-prefill table cannot be assigned is too cautious: the values are recoverable and cross-checked by Table 3. Deep-prefill rows lack a clean row in Table 2, but Table 1/4 clean values apply, since the no-prefill condition is identical. No uncertainty estimates are given. Deep prefills are 500-token harmful responses from an abliterated Gemma-3-27B.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
Tests forced assistant prefixes, including a deep prefill of 500 tokens; does not test suffix attacks or decoding changes.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether training data or objective produces shallowness.
Training to deepen safety and whether it holds up.

relation.reason: Its own undefended-model results compare fixed and deep prefilling with clean decoding and directly test V4.

tranche.reason: The study tests prefill vulnerability using harmful-continuation ASR and investigates refusal erosion through J-lens readouts, a different approach to the same safety-bypass question.

source_check.notes: All twelve proposed baseline fixes are confirmed. The authors-conclusion paraphrase overstates uniform suppression to a few percent: J-Anchor reaches 11.5% ASR on Qwen3-8B StrongREJECT under deep prefilling (Table 5; Section 5.2).
